title: Your rehat
hook: whatever stage you're at, some rule of life can be yours

segments.voice: Yesterday, rehat at work: honest earning as part of the path, and the articles of faith along for the shift. Your line was faith at work. Where did you make a little room for someone? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-eight.

Some listeners on this path wear a turban and have taken amrit. Some keep their hair and haven't. Some are learning about the faith of a partner, a grandparent, a friend at school. Some came because a line of Guru Nanak caught them and wouldn't let go. This whole block has read a code written with the initiated in mind, and it's fair to wonder where that leaves everyone else. Is a rule of life only for the people who've made the full vow? Today the path turns the code around and points it at the listener, at whatever stage you're at. Not to sign anyone up. Just to ask what a way of living looks like when it's small enough to start today.
screen: `AMRITDHARI, LEARNING, CURIOUS.` → `A CODE FOR THE INITIATED.` → `WHAT ABOUT EVERYONE ELSE?`

segments.voice: Guru Ram Das has a passage on Ang 305 that reads less like a rulebook and more like a portrait of a day. In paraphrase: the one who calls themselves a Sikh of the true Guru rises early and remembers the Name. They make the effort to bathe in the pool of nectar. Through the day they keep the Guru's word on their lips. Whatever they do, sitting or standing, they remember. And that Sikh, the passage says, is pleasing to the Guru. Look at how it's built. It's not a list of prohibitions. It's a shape: a morning, a day full of remembering, and love at the end of it. The full code we've been reading sits on top of that shape and fills it in. And the word rehat itself means a way of living, the way someone carries on day to day. Everyone has one already. A person who checks their phone first thing has a rehat. A person who skips breakfast and is short with people by noon has a rehat. The question isn't whether to have one. It's whether to choose it. So here's where the path leaves you, gently. Nobody here is being asked to take a vow. But anyone can borrow the shape of that portrait. Something for the morning. Something to carry through the day. Something to give. Three small rules, chosen on purpose, held for a while, and changed when they stop fitting. Some Sikh teachers describe the faith with three supports of their own: remember the Name, earn honestly, and share. A beginner's rule of life can be that small and still be a real one.
screen: `ANG 305: A PORTRAIT OF A SIKH'S DAY.` · `A SHAPE, NOT A LIST OF NOS.` · `EVERYONE ALREADY HAS A REHAT.` · then, large: `THREE SMALL RULES, CHOSEN ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write your own three rules. If you have paper or a phone, use it. If not, hold them in your head. One rule for the morning, the first few minutes of the day. One rule to carry, something you'll do or not do while you're out in the world. One rule for giving, of time, attention or money. Keep each to one short line. Make them small enough to keep tomorrow. Then sit with the three, and breathe with them, and notice which one already feels like yours. The bell holds the time.

Your rehat. A rehat is a way of living, and everyone has one; the question is whether to choose it. Guru Ram Das paints a Sikh's day on Ang 305: rise early, remember, keep the word on your lips. Today's word.
Your line: my three rules. Today, keep the three you wrote, even imperfectly, and tonight change one word in any rule that didn't fit. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Some Sikh teachers point to the day Guru Ram Das describes on Ang 305 (rising early, remembering the Name, keeping the Guru's word through the day) as a model of daily practice, for the initiated and for those not yet initiated.

original.note: Punjabi: a way of living, conduct; the root of rehat maryada, the Sikh code of conduct.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule of life is something only the fully committed have.
what it means: a rehat is simply a way of living, and anyone can choose theirs on purpose.
what a scholar hears: Ang 305 gives the shape of a Sikh's day as a portrait rather than a code, and the later written codes fill in that shape.
recall: the one who leads the band

sources.ref: Ang 305 (Gauri ki Var, Guru Ram Das)

notes: Ang 305–306, 'gur satgur ka jo sikh akhaae', paraphrased: rises early, meditates on the Name, bathes in the pool of nectar, keeps the Guru's word through the day, and the Guru is pleased. Please confirm the Ang and the paraphrase, especially 'the Guru loves the one who does this'.
Rehat is glossed as 'a way of living, conduct'; this is a meaning, not an etymology. Please confirm the Gurmukhi spelling ਰਹਿਤ and pronunciation.
The three supports (naam japna, kirat karni, vand chhakna) are attributed to 'some Sikh teachers'.
The practice invites the listener to write personal rules; it does not invite anyone to take amrit or make a vow, and it is not presented as Sikh rehat. Please confirm the framing is acceptable.
